learningObjectives.title: Medieval and early modern crime and punishment (c500-1700)

options: A fine paid to a victim's family as compensation
questions.explain: Wergild ('man price') compensated victims and helped prevent blood feuds.

questions.q: Trial by ordeal was used in the medieval period because people believed:
options: God would reveal a person's guilt or innocence
questions.explain: Trial by ordeal (e.g. by hot iron or water) relied on divine judgement.

questions.q: The Normans introduced Forest Laws to:
options: Protect royal hunting grounds, making many activities crimes
questions.explain: Forest Laws criminalised hunting and gathering wood in royal forests.

options: The whole community to chase and catch a suspected criminal
questions.explain: Communities were collectively responsible for catching criminals.

questions.q: 'Benefit of clergy' allowed some accused people to:
options: Be tried in more lenient Church courts
questions.explain: Those who could read a Bible passage could claim benefit of clergy and lighter punishment.

questions.q: During the 17th century, witch-hunting increased, associated with figures such as:
questions.explain: Matthew Hopkins, the self-styled 'Witchfinder General', led witch hunts amid religious upheaval.

options: The large number of crimes punishable by death
questions.explain: The Bloody Code made over 200 offences, including minor theft, capital crimes.

options: Sending them to colonies such as Australia
questions.explain: Transportation removed offenders to colonies (America, later Australia).

questions.q: Robert Peel established the Metropolitan Police in London in:
questions.explain: Peel's Metropolitan Police (1829) created Britain's first professional force ('Peelers').

questions.q: Elizabeth Fry is best known for campaigning to:
options: Improve prison conditions and reform prisoners
questions.explain: Fry promoted humane treatment and rehabilitation, especially for women prisoners.

questions.q: The Victorian 'separate system' in prisons kept prisoners:
options: Isolated in silence to encourage reflection and reform
questions.explain: The separate system emphasised isolation and moral reform (e.g. Pentonville).

questions.q: The death penalty for murder was abolished in Britain in:
questions.explain: Capital punishment for murder was abolished in 1965 (permanently in 1969).

questions.q: A major change in the aims of punishment over time has been:
options: A shift towards deterrence and rehabilitation rather than only retribution
Increasing use of trial by ordeal
questions.explain: Modern punishment increasingly emphasises rehabilitation and alternatives to prison.

questions.q: Trial by jury across the centuries is an example of:
questions.explain: Juries have persisted for centuries, illustrating continuity.

questions.q: The move from public executions to imprisonment reflects:
options: Changing attitudes towards punishment and reform
A return to the Bloody Code
questions.explain: Ending public execution shows evolving views on deterrence and humanity.

questions.q: The growth of towns and the Industrial Revolution increased the need for:
questions.explain: Urbanisation and rising crime drove the creation of professional policing.
